title: Pipelines, repositories and onboarding
summary: The shape of a promotion pipeline, how to lay out an integration repository, and the checklist for onboarding an existing API.

steps.title: The shape of the pipeline
body: Whatever the tool (Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions, GitLab), the pipeline has the same stages:
```yaml
trigger: { branches: [main], paths: [catalogue-integration/*, contracts/catalogue-*] }
stages:
- Build:        # runs on every merge
- validate the routes (camel validate / lint the contract)
- export to Maven and run the tests
- build the image, tag it with the commit id
- scan it (Trivy, Grype); fail on high/critical
- push it; publish the API project as an artifact
- Test:         # deployment job bound to the "test" environment
- run the image with test parameters and secrets
- import the API project with params-test.yaml (new revision)
- smoke-test through the gateway
- Production:   # same steps, production parameters, an approval, often a change window
Secrets come from variable groups or environment secrets linked to a vault, never from the YAML. Agents that must
reach internal registries and gateways run **inside** the network. **Rollback** is two actions: run the previous
image tag and deploy the previous API revision.

steps.prompt: Put the Build stage's steps in order.
lines: Validate the routes and lint the contract
Build the image and tag it with the commit id
Push the image and publish the API project artifact
steps.explain: Fail as early and cheaply as possible: a lint error should never cost an image build.

steps.title: Repository layout
body: Three kinds of code, three homes:
1. **Existing backends** (the catalogue service, the warehouse system) stay in **their own** repositories with
their own teams and pipelines. Nothing is copied into the integration platform: it calls them.
2. **Integration projects** live in **one integration repository**, a folder per project (a designer such as
Karavan is configured with exactly one repository and branch, and each project is a folder in it).
3. **API definitions**: contracts and gateway projects with per-environment parameters, next to the integrations.
```text
integration-platform/
contracts/            catalogue-v1.json, orders-v1.json, shipping-rates-v1.json
catalogue-integration/   one folder (one image, one service) per business domain
orders-integration/
apis/                 gateway projects + params-test.yaml / params-prod.yaml
pipelines/
README.md             naming, error contract, conventions
Note what is missing: `shipping-rates` has a contract and a gateway project but **no** integration folder: it is a pass-through.

items: The routes that reshape catalogue answers
The shared error handler used by the orders integration

steps.prompt: Someone proposes one integration project, `acme-esb`, containing every API's routes. What is the strongest argument against it?
options: Every change redeploys every API, one bad route or memory leak can take all of them down, and everything must scale together
steps.explain: Its only advantage is less setup on day one. One project per business domain (a handful, not dozens, never one per endpoint) isolates failures and owners.

steps.prompt: Onboard an existing API, in order.
lines: Get or write its OpenAPI; decide which operations consumers really need; name the service
For an integration: create the project from the contract, mock mode first, one route per operation, the shared error handler
Commit; the pipeline builds and tests the image
Import the same contract in the gateway: endpoint, scopes, plans; deploy and publish
Consumers subscribe through the developer portal
Retire the old endpoint that did the same job

steps.prompt: Which pipelines does this change trigger? What does this print?
steps.explain: Path filters keep one domain's change from rebuilding and redeploying every other domain.

steps.title: Path filters
prompt: Write `List<string> Affected(IEnumerable<string> changedFiles, Dictionary<string, string[]> pipelines)`.
Each pipeline has glob patterns; a pipeline is affected if **any** changed file matches **any** of its patterns.
Return the affected pipeline names sorted ordinally.
Glob rules (match the whole path, `/` separated, case-sensitive):
- `**` matches any number of characters, including `/`;
- everything else matches literally (`.` is a dot).
Turning a glob into an anchored regex (`Regex.Escape` the literal parts) is a good approach.
starter: List<string> Affected(IEnumerable<string> changedFiles, Dictionary<string, string[]> pipelines)
solution: List<string> Affected(IEnumerable<string> changedFiles, Dictionary<string, string[]> pipelines)
if (glob[i] == '*' && i + 1 < glob.Length && glob[i + 1] == '*') { sb.Append(".*"); i++; }
hints: Walk the glob character by character: `**` → `.*`, `*` → `[^/]*`, anything else → `Regex.Escape`.
Anchor with `^` and `$` so the whole path must match.
template: Dojo.Eq("a contract change", new List<string> { "catalogue" }, Affected(new[] { "contracts/catalogue-v1.json" }, dojoPipes));
Dojo.Eq("deep file under a project", new List<string> { "orders" }, Affected(new[] { "orders-integration/routes/create-order.camel.yaml" }, dojoPipes));
Dojo.Eq("* does not cross folders", new List<string>(), Affected(new[] { "contracts/old/catalogue-v0.json", "orders-integration.md/x" }, dojoPipes));
Dojo.Eq("several pipelines, sorted", new List<string> { "catalogue", "docs", "orders" }, Affected(new[] { "README.md", "apis/catalogue/params-prod.yaml", "contracts/orders-v2.json" }, dojoPipes));
Dojo.Eq("dots are literal", new List<string>(), Affected(new[] { "contracts/catalogue-v1xjson" }, dojoPipes));
